title: The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same | Gordon Brown
text:
When Spain goes to the polls on 29 November, its citizens will be the first of some 200 million people in Europe eligible to vote in the following 12 months; 2027 will be a year of elections – including France, Poland, Estonia and Italy – which will be critical to the future of Europe. This will be the biggest electoral test in nearly 100 years of the strength and threat of extreme rightwing populist nationalism.
Thirty years ago, around the turn of the 21st century, the left was ascendant, in charge or in coalition in 13 out of the EU’s 15 member states. Today, with Denmark the only social democratic-led government in the north of Europe, and Lithuania the only one in the east, Spain stands alongside tiny Malta as the only centre-left government in Europe’s south.
Of the EU’s 27 countries, 21 are run from the centre or right. But there is a new danger, and it is not just that another extreme rightwing populist party, Spain’s Vox, may be on the point of entering government. It is also the capitulation of the centre-right parties to far-right policies, as the firewall separating the right from the extreme right starts to fall across the continent.
Vox has proposed mass deportations of migrants under the banner of “remigration”. Spain’s Popular party (PP) has – as documented by an investigation published by LaSexta – been prepared to join with Vox in regional coalitions to remove gender-equality initiatives and minority-language protections, and to challenge abortion and LGBTQ+ protections. And although they disagree about its definition, the PP and Vox have both explicitly endorsed the principle of prioridad nacional – national preference in social security and health benefits.
Just as worrying is the rise of a global coalition of anti-internationalists. Reports of an early, unpublished version of Donald Trump’s national security strategy last year envisaged direct support being offered from the US to Europe’s extreme populist nationalist parties. The White House denied those reports, but in August, Reuters also claimed the Trump administration planned to provide at least $25m (£19m) in funding for conservative civil-society initiatives in Europe, including $4m for rightwing media.
Not content with stating via the national strategy document that Europe was threatened with “civilisational erasure”, Trump dispatched his vice-president, JD Vance, to consort with the extreme-right AfD party in Germany in preference to meeting the chancellor. Meanwhile, having convened in Hungary and the UK this year, the US-led Conservative Political Action Conference – which brings together conservative activists, commentators and officials – plans an even bigger “expansion into western Europe” with an Italian summit in 2027.
How to push back? One way is to exploit the truth: that what the far right offers isn’t necessarily in sync with what ordinary people want. Polling for the Rockefeller Foundation, of which I am a trustee, reveals the picture is much more nuanced if we ask Europeans what they are really feeling.
Spain’s statutory minimum wage has increased by two-thirds and the proportion of workers on fixed-term contracts has fallen by more than 40% under the government of Pedro Sánchez. With more than half of Spain’s electricity now coming from renewables, energy price rises have hit less hard than elsewhere in Europe, and consumer confidence has been much higher.
But Spain’s official polling agency, the Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), found that only a third give a positive assessment of the economy, while earlier this month, concerns over housing and rents led to the country’s first general strike in 14 years along with mass demonstrations on the streets of its major cities. Indeed, across Europe, half of those polled say they don’t trust their government, while two-thirds say they are nostalgic for the past, believing their countries have lost touch with the values that built them.
But these are surface manifestations of dissatisfaction. What really worries people in their daily lives? People fear economic decline – which can mean the sense that their country is doing badly (65% say theirs has got worse in the past year), as well as personal financial disappointment over the gap between their expectations and their current experience. Nearly 50% say they are worse off than they expected to be five years ago, with 59% worrying more about money every year. They also worry that nobody is there to stand up for them or speak up on their behalf. Half of respondents say that, in a crisis, people in their community would look out only for themselves. More telling, perhaps, is that half feel the government helps other groups more than theirs.
What is striking is that, for many, this sense of civic decline, which is a more cultural phenomenon, matters as much as economic decline. But while it may mean they lend their votes to populist nationalist parties that claim to speak for their concerns, most are not populist nationalists at heart. Only 15% of those voting for the radical right take a consistently zero-sum view of the world – seeing the gains of one social group as necessarily coming at the expense of another. In Spain, only 12% of Vox voters are consistently zero-sum. And a total of 61% of respondents across the European countries polled are prepared to say they want their country to cooperate internationally, even when it means compromising on national interests. Even more, 80%, reject intolerant attitudes, believing that good solutions come from hearing many different viewpoints.
What does this mean when it comes to actual votes? Across Europe, no more than 25% anywhere say they would vote for the radical right, and fewer – about 20% – see another ethnic group’s gain as their own loss. As few as 10% hold to the us-v-them mindset on trade, migration and technology that characterises the rhetoric and ideology of the populist movements. And despite the enormous publicity the issue receives, and legitimate concerns about illegal migration, fewer than 25% put managing migration among the top issues for countries to work on together.
Anti-incumbent voting is now commonplace. Millions are open to voting for change when they are dissatisfied, and may choose to protest with a vote for the extreme right. Sánchez is defending a strong record at home and abroad. Despite the day-to-day polls, Spain has one of the smallest us-v-them blocs and the lowest radical-right vote of the countries we polled, with votes destined for the extreme right standing at 14%, well short of the PP and Sánchez’s Socialists. The general public in Spain and in Europe are unhappy with their economic plight and fear the loss of civic cohesion, but they have not, in the main, become converts to far-right ideology. The drift is not inevitable. By knowing how people really feel, we can reach them.
- Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010
